items.title: Nicaea was a political project as much as a theological one
items.claim: Constantine convened the Council of Nicaea in 325 CE. What was his primary motive?

options.text: Pure theological inquiry into the nature of Christ
Political unity — the empire had recently legalised Christianity, and the Arian controversy was fracturing the church
To remove gospels he personally disliked from the Bible
To suppress the worship of Mary

items.reveal:
Constantine had legalised Christianity by the Edict of Milan (313). The Arian controversy (was the Son co-eternal with the Father, or created?) threatened civil order. Constantine wrote to Bishop Alexander and Arius effectively telling them to stop arguing.

The Council produced the Nicene Creed and condemned Arius. Constantine was baptised on his deathbed in 337 — by an Arian bishop. Theological disputes continued for decades; Athanasius was exiled five times.

The Council did NOT decide the canon of Scripture (a persistent Dan Brown myth).
items.why: Doctrines aren't formed in a vacuum. Constantine wanted a workable state religion. The metaphysics of the Trinity took shape under that pressure — neither invalidating it nor making it 'pure theology'.

items.title: Kant gave multiple formulations of the categorical imperative
items.claim: How does Kant's categorical imperative work?

options.text: One simple rule: do unto others as you would have them do to you

Multiple formulations including universalisability ('act only according to that maxim by which you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law') and humanity-as-end ('act so as to treat humanity, whether in your own person or in that of another, always as an end, never as a means only')
Whatever maximises happiness is morally required
An empirical rule derived from observation

items.reveal:
Kant's 'Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals' (1785) sets out the categorical imperative. Standard count: three formulations.

Formula of Universal Law: 'Act only according to that maxim by which you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law.'
Formula of Humanity: 'Act so as to treat humanity, whether in your own person or in that of another, always as an end, never as a means only.'
Formula of the Kingdom of Ends: 'Act according to the maxims of a member of a merely possible kingdom of ends.'

The formulations are intended to be equivalent in extension but to emphasise different aspects. Kant's most famous example (lying to the murderer at the door) shows the strict reading: lying is universally impermissible.
items.why: Kantian ethics is sometimes reduced to 'don't lie' or 'universalise your action'. The multiple formulations and the humanity-as-end principle are richer — and more humane — than the slogan suggests.

items.title: Jihad has greater and lesser meanings in classical Islam
items.claim: What is the greater/lesser jihad distinction?

options.text: Both refer only to armed warfare

A widely cited hadith distinguishes lesser jihad (armed struggle in defence of the community) from greater jihad (inner struggle against one's own ego); the hadith's authenticity is debated but the inner-struggle understanding is found in independent Sufi and mainstream piety traditions
Jihad refers only to economic struggle

items.reveal:
The Arabic root j-h-d means 'to strive, to exert effort'. The greater/lesser distinction is attributed to a hadith reported by al-Bayhaqi and al-Khatib al-Baghdadi: 'We have returned from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad — the jihad against the self.'

Ibn Taymiyya (d. 1328) and some modern scholars question the hadith's chain of authentication. But the inner-struggle theme appears widely in Sufi writing and is not dependent on the hadith alone.

Classical Islamic law (fiqh) regulates armed jihad with conditions on declaration, conduct, and protection of non-combatants — distinct from later extremist appropriations of the term.
items.why: A word picked up by 21st-century media can carry meanings that don't match its theological tradition. 'Jihad' in classical Islam is far more various than its English-language press usage.
